name: Olive Drab #7
lede: Olive Drab #7 is a near-black, brownish olive: the darker of the two US Army field-uniform shades issued from 1943, numbered within the military's own olive-drab color series.

sections.title: A darker number in a uniform series
sections.body:
*Olive* names the plant family's dull yellow-green fruit and leaf color, and *drab* is an old English cloth word for a dull, undyed brown; the US Army strung a series of numbered "olive drab" shades across its uniform specifications, from the lighter OD3 and OD33 to this darker OD7 [1]. The earlier, lighter shade proved a poor choice in the field: it stood out against most northern-European backdrops, making soldiers easier to spot, so from 1943 new uniforms and the M1943 field jacket switched to the darker OD7 for better concealment [1].

Our library carries only a Wikipedia source for this exact swatch, with no fixed year or specification number attached beyond that general military history [2]. The nearest look-alikes on file are [[indigo-tea]], a touch lighter, [[brown-olive]], duller, and [[jacaranda-brown|Jacaranda Brown]], lighter and yellower [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A close match to this near-black olive turns up in 5,220 of our 23,781 archived paintings, about 22 per cent, with the within-painting lens finding it in 4,378; that is more common than every other named color we track [3]. It most often sits as a hidden color rather than a highlight, and peaks in the 1600s at 1.2 times the archive's overall rate (1,372 paintings) [3]. Meindert Hobbema is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 11 of his 16 archived works [3]. As photographed, these are aged, varnished canvases, so a dark match like this one is partly the paint's own age, not only the pigment the painter chose [3].

origin.named_after: olive (the plant's dull green-brown color) + drab (a dull cloth color) + the U.S. Army's own shade-numbering system
origin.first_recorded: 1943, when OD7 replaced the lighter OD3/OD33 in U.S. Army field uniforms
